question:
Identify the word in the given sentence that is the ANTONYM of the word 'frugal'.
At present, people are paying extravagant prices for houses because they have to have accommodation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. extravagant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Frugal" means economical, thrifty, or careful in spending money; avoiding waste. (मितव्ययी / कम खर्च करने वाला)
◦ Example: She leads a frugal lifestyle, saving most of her salary every month.

• The word "Extravagant" means spending much more money than necessary; wasteful, which is the exact opposite of "frugal". (फिजूलखर्च)
◦ Example: His extravagant spending on parties left him in debt.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Prices" — simply means the cost of something; it is not an antonym of "frugal".

• Option 2: "Accommodation" — means lodging or housing; it is unrelated in meaning to "frugal".

• Option 3: "Present" — means the current time; it has no meaning-relationship with "frugal".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "frugal": thrifty, economical, prudent, sparing, austere.

• Other antonym pairs commonly asked by SSC: lavish ↔ frugal, generous ↔ stingy, extravagant ↔ economical.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Ignision.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Ignition" — the action of setting something alight, or the mechanism that starts an engine.
◦ Example: He turned the key in the ignition to start the car.

• Spelling key: IGNI + TION. The word ends in the suffix "-tion" (as in "action", "motion"), not "-sion". The given word "Ignision" wrongly uses "s" instead of "t".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Horticulture" — correctly spelt; the science or art of garden cultivation.

• Option 3: "Copulate" — correctly spelt; to have sexual union.

• Option 4: "Portion" — correctly spelt; a part or share of something.

NOTE

• Words ending in "-tion" vs "-sion": generally, words derived from Latin verbs ending in "-t" or "-d" take "-tion" (action, ignition, motion), while those ending in "-d" or "-s" often take "-sion" (division, decision, tension).

• Other commonly confused spellings asked by SSC: "definately" (incorrect) vs "definitely" (correct), "recieve" (incorrect) vs "receive" (correct).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
I will not go out if is raining.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. it rains.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence contains a Conditional Sentence (Type 1 / Zero Conditional) structure, introduced by "if", referring to a general/real possibility.

• Rule — Conditional sentences with "if": the "if" clause must have a subject and a verb in the Simple Present Tense; the main clause can be in the simple present or future tense.
◦ Structure: If + Subject + V1(s/es), Subject + will/shall + V1

• The given clause "if is raining" has no subject and uses the wrong verb form. It must be corrected to "if it rains", where "it" is the dummy subject used for weather, and "rains" is the correct Simple Present form.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "raining" is incorrect because it does not supply the missing subject and leaves the clause grammatically incomplete.

• Option 3: "will rain" is incorrect because the "if" clause of a conditional sentence cannot take the future tense; only the main clause can use "will".

• Option 4: "rained" is incorrect because the past tense does not fit a general/habitual condition, and it also fails to supply a subject.

NOTE

• "It" is always used as the subject for weather-related expressions in English: it is raining, it is cold, it is sunny.

• Never use two future forms ("will") in both clauses of a Type 1 conditional sentence — this is a very common SSC error-spotting trap.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.
Please ask the dog to get of my couch.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. get off my.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence uses the phrasal verb incorrectly as "get of my". The correct phrasal verb is "get off", meaning to move away from or stop standing/sitting on something.
◦ Example: Get off the table before it breaks!

• Rule: "Off" (preposition/particle, meaning away from a surface) is required here, not "of" (which shows possession or relation, e.g. "a cup of tea"). Also, since "couch" is a noun following the phrase, the possessive adjective "my" (not the possessive pronoun "mine") is needed to modify it directly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "get of mine" is incorrect — it keeps the wrong word "of" instead of "off", and also wrongly uses "mine" before a noun.

• Option 3: "get off mine" is incorrect because "mine" (possessive pronoun) cannot directly modify the noun "couch"; only "my" (possessive adjective) can be used before a noun.

• Option 4: "No substitution" is incorrect because the original sentence contains a clear grammatical error ("of" instead of "off") that must be corrected.

NOTE

• Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) are used directly before a noun, while possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs) stand alone, without a following noun.

• Other commonly confused prepositions in SSC exams: "off" vs "of", "in" vs "into", "on" vs "onto".

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
I fell / asleep while / I read / the book.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. I read.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes two actions happening at the same time in the past — falling asleep, and reading the book — joined by the conjunction "while", which indicates a background/ongoing action.

• Rule — "while" + ongoing past action: when "while" introduces a longer, ongoing action that was in progress when a shorter action occurred, the ongoing action must be in the Past Continuous Tense (was/were + V-ing), not the Simple Past.
◦ Structure: Shorter action (Simple Past) + while + Subject + was/were + V-ing

• The segment "I read" should therefore be "I was reading", since the reading was the ongoing background action during which the subject fell asleep.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the book" is grammatically correct as the object of the verb "reading/read".

• Option 3: "asleep while" is correct; "asleep" is a valid adjective complement after "fell", and "while" is the correct conjunction to join simultaneous actions.

• Option 4: "I fell" is correct; "fell" is the correct Simple Past form of "fall", used for the shorter, interrupting action.

NOTE

• "While" is regularly followed by the Past/Present Continuous Tense in SSC error-spotting questions, whereas "when" is typically followed by the Simple Past Tense for a shorter action.

• Compare: "While I was reading the book, I fell asleep" and "When I fell asleep, I was reading the book" — both are correct with continuous and simple past used appropriately.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Those streets are very lonely.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Crowded.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Lonely" means without other people; deserted, or feeling sad because one is alone. (सुनसान / अकेला)
◦ Example: He felt lonely after all his friends moved away.

• The word "Crowded" means full of people; densely occupied, which is the direct opposite of "lonely" in the context of streets. (भीड़भाड़ वाला)
◦ Example: The market was crowded with shoppers during the festival.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Isolated" is incorrect because it is a synonym of "lonely" (cut off from others), not its antonym.

• Option 3: "Empty" is incorrect because it is close in meaning to "lonely" (devoid of people), not opposite to it.

• Option 4: "Remote" is incorrect because it means far away/isolated, which is again a synonym, not an antonym, of "lonely".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "lonely": desolate, solitary, secluded, deserted, forlorn.

• Other antonym pairs frequently tested by SSC: solitary ↔ crowded, deserted ↔ populated, secluded ↔ sociable.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Concieve.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Conceive" — to form or hold an idea, plan or belief in the mind; or to become pregnant.
◦ Example: She could not conceive of a better solution to the problem.

• Spelling key: this word follows the rule "i before e, except after c". Since the word contains the letter "c", the correct order is "c-e-i" (con-cei-ve), not "c-i-e" as in the misspelt "Concieve".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Detect" — correctly spelt; to discover or identify the presence of something.

• Option 3: "Predict" — correctly spelt; to say what will happen in the future.

• Option 4: "Stimulate" — correctly spelt; to encourage development or interest.

NOTE

• The "i before e, except after c" rule also applies to words like "receive", "deceive", "perceive", and "achieve" (no "c" before, so "ie").

• Related words: conceivable, conception, misconceive — all retain the "cei" pattern.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The mob drove on the rampage and looted several shops in the locality.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. went on the rampage.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to go on the rampage" means to behave in a violent, uncontrolled and destructive manner, typically in a group. (उग्र होकर तोड़फोड़ करना)
◦ Example: The angry crowd went on the rampage, smashing shop windows and setting cars on fire.

• The verb that idiomatically collocates with "rampage" is "go" (went, in the past tense), not "drove", "played", "ran" or "strolled" — these verbs do not form a recognised idiomatic expression with "rampage".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "played on the rampage" is incorrect; "play" does not collocate with "rampage" in standard English idiom.

• Option 3: "ran on the rampage" is incorrect; while "run riot" is a valid idiom, "run on the rampage" is not the correct fixed expression.

• Option 4: "strolled on the rampage" is incorrect and self-contradictory; "stroll" suggests a calm, leisurely walk, which conflicts with the violent sense of "rampage".

NOTE

• Related idiom: "to run riot" — to behave in a wild, uncontrolled way, similar in meaning to "go on the rampage".

• Other idioms with fixed verb-noun collocations often tested by SSC: "to raise an alarm", "to strike a chord", "to draw a conclusion".

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A secret plan, made to do something (usually wrong)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Conspiracy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Conspiracy" means a secret plan made by a group of people to do something illegal or harmful, usually a wrongful act. (षड्यंत्र)
◦ Example: The police uncovered a conspiracy to smuggle goods across the border.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Strategy" means a general plan to achieve a long-term goal; it carries no sense of secrecy or wrongdoing. (रणनीति)

• Option 2: "Planning" means the general process of making plans; it is a neutral term without any secretive or unlawful connotation. (योजना बनाना)

• Option 3: "Conditioning" means training a person or animal to behave in a certain way, or getting something into a required state; it is unrelated to secret wrongful plans. (अभ्यस्त बनाना)

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: "Conspirator" — a person who takes part in a conspiracy; "Collusion" — secret agreement for a deceitful purpose.

• Similar SSC-favourite one-word substitutions: "Plot" (a secret plan, especially to do something illegal), "Intrigue" (secret plotting or scheming).

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. After a few months, the two countries engaged in the Kargil war.
B. Furthermore, a number of violent wars were fought between India and Pakistan.
C. In February 1999, during the winter invasion, India and Pakistan signed the Lahore Declaration, which was predicated on peace.
D. The engagements were extremely challenging for the Indian army since they had to fight on rough rocky terrain.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. CABD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence C is the logical opening sentence: it introduces the specific event with a date ("In February 1999...") — the signing of the Lahore Declaration — and thus sets the background/context for the paragraph.

• Sentence A follows naturally with the time-linked phrase "After a few months...", describing what happened next — the Kargil war — despite the peace declaration mentioned in C.

• Sentence B uses the linking word "Furthermore", which adds further information — generalising that many violent wars were fought between the two countries, building on the specific example (Kargil) just given in A.

• Sentence D logically concludes the paragraph, elaborating on the nature/difficulty of "the engagements" (the wars mentioned in B) — describing the challenging rocky terrain the Indian army had to fight on.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 (CABD).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (DCAB) is incorrect because it starts with "D", whose pronoun-like reference — "The engagements" — has no prior antecedent, making it an illogical opening line.

• Option 3 (CDBA) is incorrect because it places D immediately after C, but "the engagements" in D has no antecedent yet at that point in the paragraph.

• Option 4 (DABC) is incorrect for the same reason as Option 1 — it begins with D, whose reference to "the engagements" is undefined at the start.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always identify the sentence that can stand independently as an introduction (usually one with a specific date, name, or general topic statement, and no pronoun/reference needing an antecedent).

• Linking words like "Furthermore", "However", "Therefore", "Then" are strong clues to sequence — they signal what kind of sentence must have come immediately before them.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
By the skin of your teeth
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Just barely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "By the skin of your teeth" means to succeed in doing something only by a very narrow margin; just barely managing to achieve or escape something. (बहुत मुश्किल से / बाल-बाल बचना)
◦ Example: He passed the exam by the skin of his teeth, scoring just one mark above the passing limit.

• The expression originates from the Bible (Book of Job), where teeth are described as having no "skin" at all — implying an extremely narrow, almost non-existent margin.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Confident of victory" is incorrect; this describes certainty of winning, which is unrelated to the idea of a narrow escape.

• Option 2: "Kind towards the weak" is incorrect; this describes compassion, which has no connection with the idiom's meaning.

• Option 3: "Determined to strike" is incorrect; this suggests resolve to take action, which does not match the idiom's sense of a narrow margin of success.

NOTE

• Similar idioms meaning "narrowly" or "just in time": "To have a close shave", "By a hair's breadth", "To scrape through".

• Do not confuse with "To show one's teeth", which means to display aggression or hostility.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
I can't talk right now. / I am being really busy. / I'll call you later.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. I am being really busy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — "Being" with adjectives: the continuous form "am/is/are + being + adjective" is used only to describe a temporary action or behaviour that a person is consciously displaying (e.g., "He is being rude" = he is behaving rudely right now).

• "Busy" describes a state or condition, not a deliberate behaviour, so it cannot follow "being" in this sense. The correct form is simply the Simple Present Tense: "I am really busy."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "I can't talk right now" is grammatically correct; it is a simple, correctly formed negative statement in the Simple Present Tense.

• Option 3: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist in the sentence, as explained above.

• Option 4: "I'll call you later" is grammatically correct; "I'll" is a correct contraction of "I will", used correctly with a future time reference ("later").

NOTE

• "Being" is correctly used with adjectives that describe deliberate behaviour/character, e.g., "being kind", "being rude", "being careless" — but not with adjectives describing a simple physical/mental state, e.g., "busy", "tall", "hungry", "tired".

• Compare: "She is being difficult" (behaving difficult on purpose) vs. "She is tired" (a state, not behaviour — never "She is being tired").

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
To put off doing something, especially out of habitual carelessness or laziness
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Procrastinate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Procrastinate" means to delay or postpone doing something, especially out of habitual carelessness or laziness. (टालमटोल करना)
◦ Example: He always procrastinates on his assignments until the very last night before the deadline.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Accelerate" means to increase in speed or make something happen faster; it is opposite in sense to delaying something. (गति बढ़ाना)

• Option 2: "Lacerate" means to tear or deeply cut flesh or skin; it is completely unrelated in meaning. (घायल करना)

• Option 4: "Recuperate" means to recover from illness or exertion; it has no connection with delaying tasks. (स्वास्थ्य लाभ करना)

NOTE

• Related word: "Procrastination" (noun) — the act or habit of delaying tasks.

• Other similar one-word substitutes tested by SSC: "Dilatory" (tending to cause delay), "Laggard" (a person who moves or does something slowly).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Seldom had he been so joyous in other's happiness.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Frequently.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Seldom" means not often; rarely. (शायद ही कभी)
◦ Example: She seldom visits her hometown these days.

• The word "Frequently" means happening often; many times, which is the direct opposite of "seldom". (अक्सर)
◦ Example: He frequently travels abroad for business.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hardly" is incorrect because it is a synonym of "seldom" (meaning barely/scarcely), not its antonym.

• Option 2: "Rarely" is incorrect because it is also a synonym of "seldom" (meaning not often), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Occasionally" is incorrect because it means "sometimes, now and then", which is still closer to "seldom" than to its opposite, and does not carry the sense of "often" required for a true antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "seldom": rarely, hardly, scarcely, infrequently.

• Frequency-adverb scale from least to most often (useful for antonym questions): never — seldom/rarely — occasionally/sometimes — often — frequently — always.

question: Describe how you will tell your friends that Rohit helps Reghu in passive voice.
option_1: Reghu will been helped by Rohit.
option_4: Reghu is being help by Rohit.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Reghu is helped by Rohit.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Rohit helps Reghu" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5(s/es) + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "Reghu" becomes the subject; since it is singular/third person, the auxiliary used is "is"; the verb "helps" becomes the past participle "helped"; and "Rohit" becomes the agent introduced with "by".
◦ Passive: Reghu is helped by Rohit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Reghu will been helped by Rohit" is incorrect; it is grammatically malformed — "will" must be followed by a base verb ("be helped"), not "been", and it wrongly introduces the future tense, which is not present in the active sentence.

• Option 3: "Rohit help Reghu" is incorrect because it is not even in the passive voice — it remains an active sentence, and it is also grammatically wrong ("help" should be "helps" for third-person singular subject "Rohit").

• Option 4: "Reghu is being help by Rohit" is incorrect because the past participle "helped" has been wrongly written as the base form "help", and "is being" would incorrectly signal the present continuous tense.

NOTE

• Only transitive verbs (verbs that take an object) can be converted into the passive voice; intransitive verbs (e.g., "sleep", "arrive") cannot form a passive.

• Always check that the past participle (V3) form of the main verb is used correctly when converting to passive voice — a very common SSC distractor is to leave the verb in its base form.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
They are playing songs so ________that the entire neighbourhood is disturbed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. loud.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — "so...that" construction: the structure "so + adjective/adverb + that" is used to show a result or consequence of a high degree of some quality.
◦ Structure: Subject + Verb + so + Adjective + that + Result Clause

• The blank requires an adjective describing the songs — "loud" (meaning producing a high volume of sound) is the correct word that logically causes the neighbourhood to be disturbed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "lord" is a noun (a title/ruler) and makes no grammatical or logical sense in the blank.

• Option 2: "loved" is the past tense/participle of "love"; it does not fit the sense of noise disturbing the neighbourhood.

• Option 3: "laud" is a verb meaning "to praise"; it cannot function as an adjective describing the songs.

NOTE

• Do not confuse these commonly mistaken homophone-like words: "loud" (noisy), "laud" (to praise), "lord" (a nobleman/ruler), "lured" (attracted/enticed).

• "So...that" is often confused with "such...that": "so" is followed directly by an adjective/adverb, while "such" is followed by a noun phrase (e.g., "It was such a loud song that everyone woke up").

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice
The cards were being distributed by her to her friends.
option_1: She was distributing the cards to her friends.
option_2: Her friends were distributing the cards for her.
option_3: The cards were been distributed to her friends.
option_4: Her cards were distributed by her friends.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. She was distributing the cards to her friends.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The cards were being distributed by her to her friends" is in the Past Continuous Tense, Passive Voice.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + being + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + was/were + V-ing + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "by her" becomes the subject "She"; the auxiliary "were being" with past participle "distributed" becomes "was distributing" (since the subject "she" is singular); and the object "the cards" remains the object, with "to her friends" retained as it was.
◦ Active: She was distributing the cards to her friends.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Her friends were distributing the cards for her" is incorrect because it wrongly makes "her friends" (the indirect object) the subject, distorting the original meaning — the original sentence indicates "she" was the one distributing, not her friends.

• Option 3: "The cards were been distributed to her friends" is incorrect because it is grammatically malformed passive construction ("were been" is not valid) and is not even in the active voice as required.

• Option 4: "Her cards were distributed by her friends" is incorrect because it again incorrectly swaps the subject and agent, changing the meaning and remaining in the passive voice.

NOTE

• The past continuous passive structure "was/were + being + V3" must convert to the active past continuous structure "was/were + V-ing" — a common SSC error is leaving the participle unchanged.

• Always match the number/person of the new subject (agent) with the correct form of "was/were" when converting passive to active voice.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
He brought disgrace to his family by being involved in illegal activities.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Honour.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Disgrace" means loss of reputation or respect as the result of a dishonourable action; shame. (अपमान / बदनामी)
◦ Example: His dishonest behaviour brought disgrace upon the entire family.

• The word "Honour" means high respect or great esteem; a good reputation, which is the direct opposite of "disgrace". (सम्मान)
◦ Example: She brought honour to her country by winning the gold medal.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Suspicion" is incorrect because it means a feeling of doubt or mistrust, which is unrelated in meaning to "disgrace".

• Option 2: "Shame" is incorrect because it is a synonym of "disgrace" (a painful feeling due to wrongdoing), not its antonym.

• Option 3: "Discord" is incorrect because it means disagreement or conflict, which is not opposite in meaning to "disgrace".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "disgrace": shame, dishonour, ignominy, humiliation, infamy.

• Other antonym pairs often tested by SSC: dishonour ↔ honour, infamy ↔ fame, humiliation ↔ dignity.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Divergence
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Convergence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Divergence" means the process of developing in different directions; moving apart from a common point. (विचलन / भिन्नता)
◦ Example: There was a clear divergence of opinion between the two committee members.

• The word "Convergence" means the process of coming together and meeting at a common point, which is the direct opposite of "divergence". (अभिसरण / एकत्रीकरण)
◦ Example: The convergence of the two rivers creates a spectacular natural sight.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Existence" is incorrect; it means the state of being real or alive, and has no direct relation to "divergence".

• Option 3: "Resilience" is incorrect; it means the ability to recover quickly from difficulties, unrelated in meaning to "divergence".

• Option 4: "Transience" is incorrect; it means the quality of lasting only for a short time, which is not opposite in meaning to "divergence".

NOTE

• Related verb-noun pairs: "diverge" (verb) → "divergence" (noun); "converge" (verb) → "convergence" (noun).

• Other antonym pairs based on the root "verge" often tested: divergent ↔ convergent, diverse ↔ uniform.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who gives help and sympathy to people who need it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Samaritan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Samaritan" (or "Good Samaritan") means a person who gives help and sympathy to people who are in trouble or need it. (परोपकारी व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: A kind Samaritan stopped to help the injured cyclist on the highway.

• The term originates from the Biblical parable of the Good Samaritan, who helped a wounded stranger when others ignored him.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Preacher" means a person who delivers religious sermons; it does not specifically mean someone who helps the needy. (उपदेशक)

• Option 2: "Moralist" means a person who teaches or promotes a system of morals, often seen as preachy; it does not mean a helper of the needy. (नीतिशास्त्री)

• Option 4: "Pardoner" historically referred to a person authorised to sell indulgences/pardons; it has no connection to helping people in need.

NOTE

• Related expression: "Good Samaritan law" — laws that protect people who help others in an emergency from legal liability.

• Other people-related one-word substitutes tested by SSC: "Philanthropist" (a person who promotes the welfare of others through charity), "Altruist" (a person who is unselfishly concerned for the welfare of others).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Maasais live in (1)_________ very beautiful part of Africa. They live on the wide plains in southern and northern Kenya and northern Tanzania. The area (2)________ of miles of rolling grass land, on which you can find thorny bushes and rocky hills. The people move from one place to another according to the seasons, looking for grasses and other plants (3)_________ which their cattle can graze. They have no permanent home. When they want to settle in a place for some time, they build a kind of camp called a ‘Manyatta’, where a few families live for a (4)_________ weeks or months. Then they move on again, taking their few (5)________ with them, and burning the old ‘Manyatta’ to the ground.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. a.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires the indefinite article "a" before the phrase "very beautiful part of Africa", since "part" is a singular, countable noun being introduced for the first time.

• Rule — Articles: the indefinite article "a" is used before a singular countable noun when it is mentioned for the first time or does not refer to something specific.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "that" is incorrect; "that" is a demonstrative pronoun/determiner used to point to something specific already known, which does not fit here.

• Option 3: "their" is incorrect; "their" is a possessive adjective, and there is no plural noun antecedent for it to refer to in this context.

• Option 4: "some" is incorrect; "some" is generally used with plural or uncountable nouns, not with a singular countable noun like "part".

NOTE

• Use "a" before words beginning with a consonant sound, and "an" before words beginning with a vowel sound, regardless of the actual first letter (e.g. "an hour", "a university").

• Articles are one of the most frequently tested topics in SSC cloze-test passages — always check whether the noun is singular/plural, countable/uncountable, and specific/non-specific before choosing.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Maasais live in (1)_________ very beautiful part of Africa. They live on the wide plains in southern and northern Kenya and northern Tanzania. The area (2)________ of miles of rolling grass land, on which you can find thorny bushes and rocky hills. The people move from one place to another according to the seasons, looking for grasses and other plants (3)_________ which their cattle can graze. They have no permanent home. When they want to settle in a place for some time, they build a kind of camp called a ‘Manyatta’, where a few families live for a (4)_________ weeks or months. Then they move on again, taking their few (5)________ with them, and burning the old ‘Manyatta’ to the ground.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. consists.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — "consist of": the phrasal verb "consist of" means to be made up of; to be composed of, and is used to describe what something contains or comprises.
◦ Structure: Subject (singular) + consists of + Noun/Noun Phrase

• Since "the area" is a singular subject, the correct verb form is "consists" (third person singular, Simple Present Tense), giving "The area consists of miles of rolling grass land."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "surrounds" is incorrect; "surround" means to be positioned all around something, which does not logically fit — the area cannot "surround miles of" land in this sense.

• Option 2: "measures" is incorrect; while "measures" could describe size, it does not fit idiomatically with "of miles of rolling grass land" the way "consists of" does.

• Option 3: "considers" is incorrect; "consider" means to think about something carefully, which makes no logical sense as a description of an area of land.

NOTE

• "Consist of" is never used in the passive voice or continuous tense (we do not say "is being consisted of").

• Related expressions: "comprise" (the whole comprises the parts, used without "of"), "be composed of", "be made up of" — all similar in meaning to "consist of".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Maasais live in (1)_________ very beautiful part of Africa. They live on the wide plains in southern and northern Kenya and northern Tanzania. The area (2)________ of miles of rolling grass land, on which you can find thorny bushes and rocky hills. The people move from one place to another according to the seasons, looking for grasses and other plants (3)_________ which their cattle can graze. They have no permanent home. When they want to settle in a place for some time, they build a kind of camp called a ‘Manyatta’, where a few families live for a (4)_________ weeks or months. Then they move on again, taking their few (5)________ with them, and burning the old ‘Manyatta’ to the ground.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a preposition that logically completes the phrase **"looking for grasses and other plants ______ which their cattle can graze"**.

• Rule — Preposition "on" with "graze": cattle are said to "graze on" grass or plants — meaning they feed on growing vegetation while it is still in the ground. The relative structure "plants on which... can graze" is equivalent to "plants which... can graze on".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "by" is incorrect; "graze by" is not an idiomatically correct combination for describing cattle feeding on plants.

• Option 3: "with" is incorrect; "graze with" does not correctly express the idea of feeding on vegetation.

• Option 4: "at" is incorrect; "graze at" is not the standard preposition used with this verb in this sense.

NOTE

• "Graze" can also be used without a preposition as a transitive-like verb in casual usage ("the cattle graze the fields"), but in formal/relative clause constructions like this one, "graze on" is the standard idiomatic form.

• Prepositions with common verbs are a frequently tested cloze-test topic in SSC exams — it is useful to learn fixed verb-preposition collocations (e.g., "depend on", "look for", "graze on", "feed on") by heart.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Maasais live in (1)_________ very beautiful part of Africa. They live on the wide plains in southern and northern Kenya and northern Tanzania. The area (2)________ of miles of rolling grass land, on which you can find thorny bushes and rocky hills. The people move from one place to another according to the seasons, looking for grasses and other plants (3)_________ which their cattle can graze. They have no permanent home. When they want to settle in a place for some time, they build a kind of camp called a ‘Manyatta’, where a few families live for a (4)_________ weeks or months. Then they move on again, taking their few (5)________ with them, and burning the old ‘Manyatta’ to the ground.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. few.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes an indefinite, small number of "weeks or months" — a plural countable noun phrase.

• Rule — "a few" with plural countable nouns: the phrase "a few" means "a small number of" and is used before plural countable nouns to indicate a modest but sufficient quantity. Here it exactly parallels the earlier phrase in the same sentence, "a few families live...", maintaining consistency of style.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "little" is incorrect; "little" (without "a") is used with uncountable nouns and to mean "hardly any", which is unsuitable before the plural countable noun "weeks or months".

• Option 2: "significant" is incorrect; while grammatically an adjective could fit, "a significant weeks or months" is grammatically wrong, as "significant" cannot combine naturally with the indefinite article and the informal, general sense the passage requires.

• Option 3: "least" is incorrect; "least" is a superlative form used for the smallest amount/degree, and "a least weeks or months" is not a grammatically valid phrase.

NOTE

• Distinguish: "a few" (a small positive number — some) vs. "few" (almost none, negative sense) — e.g., "a few people came" (some did) vs. "few people came" (hardly any did).

• "A little" and "little" show the same countable/uncountable and positive/negative distinction, but are used with uncountable nouns (e.g., "a little water" vs. "little water").

The Maasais live in (1)_________ very beautiful part of Africa. They live on the wide plains in southern and northern Kenya and northern Tanzania. The area (2)________ of miles of rolling grass land, on which you can find thorny bushes and rocky hills. The people move from one place to another according to the seasons, looking for grasses and other plants (3)_________ which their cattle can graze. They have no permanent home. When they want to settle in a place for some time, they build a kind of camp called a ‘Manyatta’, where a few families live for a (4)_________ weeks or months. Then they move on again, taking their few (5)________ with them, and burning the old ‘Manyatta’ to the ground.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. belongings.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a noun describing what the Maasais take with them when they move to a new location — "belongings" means personal possessions, especially small, portable items. (सामान / निजी वस्तुएं)
◦ Example: The refugees carried only a few belongings as they fled their homes.

• The context — "taking their few ______ with them, and burning the old 'Manyatta' to the ground" — clearly indicates physical possessions being carried away before the old camp is destroyed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "inhibitions" is incorrect; it means psychological restraints or shyness, which cannot logically be "taken" while moving camp.

• Option 2: "experiences" is incorrect; while people do carry memories/experiences, this is not a concrete or contextually fitting word for describing physical items packed for a move.

• Option 3: "antiques" is incorrect; it means old, valuable collectible objects, which is too specific and not supported by the passage's context of a nomadic people's simple camp.

NOTE

• "Belongings" is always used in the plural form to mean personal possessions; there is no singular form with the same meaning ("a belonging" is not standard usage).

• Similar vocabulary often tested in comprehension passages: "possessions", "effects" (personal effects), "paraphernalia", "chattels".
